---
title: "Alt text that ships with the plot"
description: "Every vellumplot writes a text alternative into the file it renders: role=\"img\" and a <desc> in SVG, a tagged Figure in PDF. plot_alt() shows you what a screen reader will read."
categories: [Accessibility]
image: figs/accessibility.png
---

```{r}
#| include: false
source("_helper.R")
library(palmerpenguins)
pen <- penguins[complete.cases(penguins), ]
```

A chart with no text alternative is invisible to anyone using a screen reader.
Most plotting libraries leave that gap for you to fill by hand, so in practice
it stays empty. vellumplot fills it by default: every plot carries a written
description, and that description travels into the rendered file.

The data is the 333 complete [Palmer Penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/).

```{r}
p <- vplot(pen) |>
  mark_point(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species, size = 2) |>
  labs(title = "Flipper length vs. body mass",
       x = "flipper length (mm)", y = "body mass (g)", color = "species")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
vg(p, "accessibility")
```

## What a screen reader gets

`plot_alt()` returns the description vellumplot will attach. You did not write
one, so it built the sentence from the specification: the chart type, what each
axis and the colour encode, and how many observations went in.

```{r}
plot_alt(p)
```

That summary is honest but mechanical. It reports the encoding, not the finding.
When the point of the chart is a pattern, write the pattern yourself with
`labs(alt = ...)` and vellumplot uses your text verbatim.

```{r}
p <- p |>
  labs(alt = paste(
    "Body mass rises with flipper length across all three penguin species.",
    "Gentoo penguins cluster in the upper right as the largest on both",
    "measures, while Adelie and Chinstrap overlap in the lower left."
  ))

plot_alt(p)
```

## It ends up in the file

The description is not metadata you have to remember to export. When the plot
renders, it goes into the file. An SVG gets `role="img"` and an
`aria-labelledby` that points at the title and the description, so assistive
technology reads the title as the chart's name and the `<desc>` as its content.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| class-output: default
dir.create("figs", showWarnings = FALSE)
render_plot(p, "figs/accessibility.svg", dpi = 150)
svg <- paste(readLines("figs/accessibility.svg"), collapse = "\n")
svg_open <- regmatches(svg, regexpr("<svg[^>]*>", svg))
title <- regmatches(svg, regexpr("<title[^<]*</title>", svg))
desc  <- regmatches(svg, regexpr("<desc[^<]*</desc>", svg))
cat(svg_open, "\n  ", title, "\n  ", desc, "\n  ...\n</svg>\n", sep = "")
```

The title comes from `labs(title = ...)` and becomes the accessible name; the
`<desc>` is whatever `plot_alt()` returns. Render the same plot to PDF and the
chart is tagged as a `Figure` whose `Alt` is that text, which is what a
PDF reader announces and what a tagging checker looks for.

Because the description comes from the spec, you can read it back in R, in the
console, before anything is drawn. So you can review it, or test it, the way you
would any other output.

```{r}
#| eval: false
testthat::expect_match(plot_alt(p), "flipper length")
```

See the [Accessibility article](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/) in the
vellumplot docs for the full treatment, including how the description handles
faceting and layered marks.
